The scientific methods in the practice of biology. The success of reductionist approach to problems in molecular biology. Contrast with holistic (higher level) biology. Resurgence of interest in global approaches like- systems biology, complexity and various “Omics”. Richness of biology in cyclical phenomena with interdependent parallel processes, feedback loops and networks. Emergent properties of the system. The concept of Causality in light of extant complexity. Complexity and indeterminacy in Biology. Historical contingency and evolution. History, nature and the future of Biology: Physics-biology interface during the classical period; biology as an independent science during the 19th and 20th centuries (the major concepts and their evolution); the nature of explanation in modern biology; the future directions. The interface between Biology (Genetics) and Society: some controversies. Darwinism, Lamarckism and Creationism; Eugenics, its history and future; ELSIfication of biology. Genetic screening; Evolution of ethics and ethics in post-genomic society. Bio-safety and environmental concerns. Molecular organizing principles of living systems. Ontogenic theories based on molecular self-organization. Importance of template replication and macromolecular catalysis. Protein first or DNA first conundrum. RNA world hypothesis. Present consensus and remaining challenges.

Description: Course Objectives: 1. Introduce soil as a three-phase engineering material 2. Encourage students to apply concepts from engineering and solid mechanics to quantify stresses in soil 3. Familiarize students with steady and transient flow through soils 4. Make students acquainted with soil’s reaction to external loading under various drainage scenario 5. Expose students to the concepts of strength and deformation of soils Learning Outcomes: At the end of the semester students should be able to • calculate various weight and volume indices for soils • classify soil based on its grain characteristics and index properties • analyze and quantify the effects of steady-state seepage (flow) through soil • calculate geostatic and induced (by external loading) stresses at any point within the ground • analyze compaction characteristics of soil • calculate degree of consolidation at any time after load placement • calculate settlement due to soil consolidation • quantify soil shear strength parameters under drained and undrained conditions • calculate shear strength of fine-grained and coarse-grained soils employing simple constitutive relation Course Content: • Origin and characteristics of soils, physical properties and soil classification. Phase relationships and soil compaction. Effective stress and soil capillarity. Soil permeability, seepage force, 1D flow and 2D flow nets. Stress distribution using the theory of elasticity and soil consolidation. Mohr circles, shear strength and failure criterion. Stress paths and routine laboratory tests to determine undrained and drained shear strength.

Description: This course is based on selected topics in mechanism design. Description: The topics covered will include the following: 1) Medical imaging modalities * Mathematical imaging models for physical quantities, sampling, noise models, artifact models. * X-ray, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion MRI, functional MRI, positron-emission tomography (PET), microscopy, ultrasound, 2D imaging, 3D/volume imaging, dynamic imaging. 2) Data visualization * Sectioning, multimodal images, overlays, rendering surfaces and volumes, glyphs, tools, applications in medical image computing. 3) Image models * Statistical models of image intensities, geometric models for images, implicit representations, geometric deformable models, Markov random fields, statistical models of texture, learning models from image data, applications in medical image computing. 4) Image reconstruction * Practical data sampling and acquisition schemes in medical imaging, inverse transforms, mathematical formulations, iterative reconstruction algorithms. 5) Image restoration * Mathematical models for degraded and missing data, Bayesian graphical modeling, Bayesian inference, learning-based methods, applications in medical image computing. 6) Image segmentation, object delineation, image classification. * Clustering methods, classification, mixture models, graph partitioning, variational methods, expectation maximization, hidden Markov random fields, applications in medical image computing. 7) Statistical shape analysis * Shape descriptors, shape spaces, shape distances, learning statistical models of shape variability, hypothesis testing, other applications in medical image computing. 8) Image registration * Spatial-deformation models, image-similarity models, mathematical formulations and optimization algorithms, co-registration, motion correction, atlas construction, other applications in medical image computing. 9) Kernel methods in medical imaging * Implicit feature spaces, kernel functions, Hilbert spaces, modeling variability in feature spaces, regression models, applications. 10) Deep learning for medical image analysis * Deep neural networks, adversarial components in learning, autoencoders, variational inference, deep generative modeling, applications. ** The course will offer hands-on experience through several computing experiments that will explore the characteristics and behavior of the theories and algorithms on real-world medical image data in clinical/scientific applications. The computing experiments will rely on Matlab/Python/C++ environments for file input/output, data processing, and data visualization. Students will code up key algorithms covered in the lectures, and other related algorithms, for empirical analyses using openly available datasets on the internet.

Description: In the first half of the semester, I plan to introduce dynamics of the complex networks. This will mainly deal with (i) various graph generative models, (ii) simple link prediction methods and (iii) diffusion processes on networks. More specifically, 1. Overview of network science in the context of real life networks, and limitations of classical graph theory to address them. 2. Generative models on graphs:--- Classical (physics based) random graph generative models--- Price model, Barabasi Albert model and Erdos-Renyl model, with their statistical properties and generating functions. --- Modern graph generative models– Kronecker and Forest Fire models. Inference of Kronecker graphs. Difference between Forest Fire and Price models 3. Link prediction heuristics: Adamic adar, jaccard coefficients, supervised random walk 4. Processes over networks: Classical information cascade models, epidemic processes and their application on viral marketing. In the second half of the semester, I plan to introduce deep learning on graphs. In particular, 1. Representation learning of graphs--- Various node representation methods e.g. Node2Vec, LINE, DeepWalk. 2. Inductive node representation methods-- GraphSAGE and graph convolutional network 3. Graph neural networks 4. Deep generative models on graphs--- variational autoencoder on graphs and generative adversarial networks on graphs.

Description: 1. Review of the basics of deep learning models, architectures and terminologies, including transformers, emphasizing the nature of the workload (e.g., matrix operations, attention matrix computation, FLOPS and memory requirements). 2. Overview of modern GPU architectures. GPU performance and resource usage in the context of deep learning, e.g., concepts of arithmetic intensity, ops:bytes ratio, compute bound vs memory bound workloads, Hardware-aware optimizations for DL workloads, e.g., tiling for matrix operations. 3. Programming frameworks (e.g., Tensorflow, PyTorch) and compilers for Al/ML systems. 4. Hardware-aware and software-defined optimizations: KV caching, efficient attention algorithms (FlashAttention, Rabe-Staats), compressed DL models (pruning, quantization, parameter sharing, knowledge distillation). 5. Training and inference at scale: Parallel and distributed techniques for training (data parallelism, pipeline parallelism, federated learning, case studies of a large model training (e.g. LLama3 paper, DeepSeek). High-performance LLM inferencing servers and deployments: KV cache memory allocation optimizations, reuse optimizations, batching, parallelism, offload, request scheduling. 6. Lab exercises: Hands-on exercises on CUDA programming, building ML pipelines (e.g., for LLM inference) in PyTorch, and measuring the performance impact of various systems techniques studied in the course. The course may include a project component that encourages students to explore further aspects of this topic.

Description: {Background:} Markov Chains and regenerative processes have been extensively used in modeling a wide variety of systems and phenomena. Likewise, many systems can be modeled as queueing systems with some aspect of the queue governed by a random process. Obvious examples of such systems occur in telecommunication systems, manufacturing systems and computer systems. This course is aimed at teaching system modeling using Markov chains with special emphasis on developing queueing models. The course contents are as follows. Introduction: Review of basic probability, properties of nonnegative random variables, laws of large numbers and the Central Limit Theorem Renewal Processes: Basic definitions, recurrence times, rewards and renewal reward theorem, point processes, Poisson process, Walds equation, Blackwell`s theorem Discrete time Markov chains: definitions and properties, matrix representation, Perron-Frobenius theory Continuous time Markov chains: basic definitions, $Q-$matrix, birth-death processes, quasi birth death processes. Description: This course deals with advanced antenna and propagation channel concepts for multipleantenna-based and millimeter-wave-based communications. With the commercial launch of the Fifth Generation of Mobile Radio Networks (5G) in 2020, antenna engineers need more than ever to be aware of physical layer strategies that are currently considered to reach the expected performance. With techniques such as MIMO and millimeter-wave communications, new challenges arise and antenna engineers cannot afford anymore to be only expert in electromagnetics, but do also require skills regarding propagation channel, digital modulations, and coding aspects. New communications schemes use advanced signal processing and coding techniques in order to exploit as much as possible the propagation channel to maximize some metrics such as the capacity. The antenna being a part of the channel, its properties influence the overall performance, and knowledge of physical layer features is therefore of utmost importance in the antenna design. This course addresses important theoretical concepts in the field of antennas and propagation in the context of 5G communications. The first unit of the course introduces physical layer aspects that have to be considered while designing antenna solutions. The second unit tackles MIMO aspects and how antenna performance should be specifically assessed accordingly. The third unit illustrates some specific issues related to vehicular and ehealth applications. The fourth unit introduces the challenges faced while using millimeterwaves for communications. This unit IV also addresses in detail two advanced antenna technologies, namely, leaky-wave antennas and Substrate-Integrated-Waveguide-based antennas. It is to be noted that theoretical concept in this course are not limited to 5G communications and are therefore useful to any antenna engineer.

Description: ENT603 Introduction to Innovation & Entrepreneurship: It is a great time to create value and to create jobs in emerging economies as an entrepreneur. This activity-oriented foundation course provides the necessary context and content for learners interested in innovation and entrepreneurship. Learners will gain an understanding of the Entrepreneurial process – the entrepreneurial mindset, opportunity identification and innovation, customer discovery and Go-To-Market, entrepreneurial finance, and technology venture creation. This course will use a combination of concept teaching and real-life storytelling to bring alive the entrepreneurial journey for learners. Learners can apply the principles and practices taught through a hands-on course project. There have been ventures created by students who have taken this course, and some of them will be covered as case studies. Course instruction is by a faculty team who bring in experience and expertise in entrepreneurship, academia, industry. Learning Objectives: (1) Getting into the entrepreneurial mindset (2) Gaining an understanding of the innovation and entrepreneurship process (3) Recognizing opportunities for new business (4) Getting hands-on during the Customer Discovery Process (5) Understanding Technology evolution and product and business life-cycles (6) Gaining insights into startup financing (7) Understanding of business functions essential for success of technology enterprises.

Description: "The aim of the course is to expose students to social enterprise and inclusive business and provide an introduction to the concepts, theory and practice of social entrepreneurship, social innovation and social impact and give students a sense of what these different ideas and concepts mean, how they are put into practice, and how they create social value in society. By doing this course, students will gain a deeper appreciation of social innovation, social entrepreneurship, inclusive business practices as well as more conventional business activities to create social impact, such as CSR & ESG, and a better understanding of the discourses and debates around these topics. Students learn about different kinds of social enterprises, using case studies, and look at how business are increasingly focused on social and sustainable business models. An additional aim is to make students excited about social innovation, social entrepreneurship and inclusive business practices, and get them to think about how they may wish to apply some of these ideas in their ventures. Learning outcomes include understanding different types of social enterprises, being able to critically assess them and understand how they are different from regular startups and businesses, becoming aware of how and why working with low-income consumers and beneficiaries can be challenging, and how to adapt. These learning outcomes will be achieved with a mixture of lectures, case study discussions, group exercises, and course project work, and assessed through assignments, and exams.succeed. This course introduces the Fundamentals of Business to the learners." "Social Innovation & Social Entrepreneurship: theoretical underpinnings 1. Social Enterprise models: Agriculture, Health, Education, Financial Services, Sanitation 2. Understanding low-income customers/ consumers + Inclusive Markets 3. Measuring the impact of social enterprises 4. Scaling social enterprises: challenges in growing and replicating impact 5. Supporting social enterprises: impact investors, blended finance and philanthropy 6. Inclusive Business: Business at the Base of the Pyramid (BoP) ESG, Corporate Social Responsibility"

Description: Many of India`s most successful entrepreneurial companies have been substantially influenced by Angels in the early stage and professionally managed venture capital subsequently for growth. This relationship is examined from both the entrepreneur`s and the venture capitalist`s perspective. From the point of view of the entrepreneur, the course considers how significant business opportunities are identified, planned, and built into sustainable companies; how resources are matched with opportunity; and how, within this framework, founders seek capital and partner with Angels / venture capitalists for value creation . From the point of view of the venture capitalist, the course considers how potential entrepreneurial investments are evaluated, valued, structured, and incentivised for; how different venture capital strategies are deployed; and how venture capitalists raise and manage their own funds. The course includes a term-long project where students work in teams (4-5 students per team) to assess and structure a multi stage funding plan that meets both founder and Venture Capitalists goals.

Description: 1. Disciplinary approaches to the pastThis module explores the emergence and consolidation of the disciplines of history and archaeology in modern times. It comparessome older forms of engaging with the past with the discipline of history as we know it today. How did the idea of history achieve such centrality in everyday discourse? The module probes intoquestions such as what is a historical fact, what gets recorded as history and what is left out, the questions of historical objectivity andthe relations between 302221facts302222 and 302221interpretation302222. This module also explores how archaeologists study past human cultures through material remains. What does it mean to be an archaeologist? How isarchaeology different from fascination for and collection of past objects? The module will look at how archaeology emerged as a modern discipline. Focusing on the questions that archaeologists ask,and through case studies, the module will explore how archaeologists recover, record and interpret material remains.2. Traces of the Past - Literary, Material, OralThe central question of this unit is: How do archaeologists and historians think and write about the past? It will introduce the concept of traces of the past and examine how they are located,analysed and read. It will explore which traces of the past literary, material, oral, visual, aural302227survive, why they do, and who their creators were. It will further ask whether it is possible todevelop a comprehensive understanding of our past by studying these traces of the past. This unit will also address the limitationsinvolved in understanding the past through them.3. Chronology, Temporality, Periodization These are some of the frameworks by which these disciplines have been construed, researched and understood. Recent works explore the need to look at these concepts differently. Using interdisciplinaryframeworks and case studies, the course will delve into the idea of time with respect to the past.4. Remembering the Past in the PresentThe past is continually interpreted and engaged with in the present by both historians and the public. This unit will explore the diverse sites where historical inquiry and public engagement with historyand past takes place every day. Drawing on global examples, it will offer critical insights into contemporary perceptions of the past,historical narratives, and collective memory.5.Sites of the Past This module will explore various sites of the past: archives, museums, monuments and memorials. The unit will provide studentsa comprehensive understanding of the structure, function and nature of these sites, as well as the ways in which the past is encountered,represented and narrated through them.

Description: The course will have three core sections: 1. Archaeology, Landscapes and the Human Past : Archaeology has long been exploring ways of understanding human-land interactions. While earlier work concentrated on how humans over time have exploited the resources on and off the landscapes, later research tried to better understand how humans perceived the landscape. This part of the course will outline some of the different perspectives in order to understand the relationship between humans, the landscape and technological changes over time. 2. Paleobiological studies and the Landscape : This segment explores how paleobiological evidence - from fossil pollen to ancient animal remains - helps reconstruct past landscapes and ecosystems. Students will learn how human activities, from early hunting to agriculture and metallurgy, left lasting imprints on biodiversity, climate, and geography over tens of thousands of years. Using case studies from Ice Age extinctions, ancient river systems, and collapsed civilizations, we will examine how landscape changes influenced natural selection and species survival. The module also introduces practical techniques like microfossil analysis and paleoenvironmental mapping to trace the deep-time dynamics between humans, climate, and the biosphere. This foundation will prepare students to critically assess both ancient and modern patterns of human-environment interaction. 3. Geospatial Technologies : Geospatial technologies offer powerful tools and techniques for archaeological studies. This module will introduce the audience about the basics of geospatial technologies especially from a data collection perspective. The topics that will be covered are: Maps and its characteristics, Land Surveying, Remote Sensing and basic geospatial analysis using open-source tools.

Description: Understanding the domain of needs and values. Examine the history and development of sustainability as a social goal through 3P diagram and explore its implications for the design of built environments. Study concepts such as life-cycle analysis both in manmade systems and in nature, biomimicry, natural capitalism, cradle-to-cradle production, unfolding wholeness, and ecological design. In addition to the latest tools, techniques, and materials, you explore government programs, legislation, industry regulations and codes, green certifications, LEED, and nonprofit organizations involved with sustainability. Solve design problem in sustainability context and experience how a new window on innovation opens up. Translate your knowledge of sustainable design concepts into practical, deployable, and tangible methods. Learn to take responsibility for your work by understanding the impact that your designs have on the environment and how to control this impact. Through research of materials, systems, and manufacturing / construction methods, you explore ways to design and build in an environmentally responsible manner. Using case studies, you look at how others are creating communities, solving economic problems, and developing new solutions to design. Class involves lectures, discussions, and student presentations exploring these ideas.

Description: This course will introduce students to theoretical perspectives and methods used in the critical design process. The course would introduce various theoretical perspectives in design in relation to the socio-cultural issues of the present, structured around thematic areas of investigation. Students will learn to use theoretical lenses to define, analyse, and explain design artefacts. Through these lenses, students will explore questions such as, How does design and the designer interact with specific social phenomena? How do they influence each other? and, How are existing social structures mediated and propagated through design? Specific theories that the course will cover include: Semiotics and Communication, Labour and Work, Language and Power, Gender and Gendering, Universalism and Regionalism etc. Over all This course will guide students to: • Analyse design interventions through various historical and theoretical lenses. • Develop awareness towards diverse narratives of power, identity, representation, technology, sustainability, agency, and several other such issues. • Engage in critical dialogue to understand the social, cultural, environmental, and ethical implications of design objects and practices. Throughout the course, real-life examples will be used to illustrate and explain theories.

Description:     9.      Impartial Games and Perfect Play Outcomes: Normal play convention is last move wins. 2 players have the same options; the position space can be partitioned into two outcome classes: Previous- or Next- player win. Sprague Grundy Theory: Every impartial normal play game is equivalent with a nim heap. Partizan Games: Players have different sets of options. Four partially ordered Outcome classes, player Previous, Next, Left or Right wins. Game Comparison: The set of all games together with defined game addition is a partially ordered group. This induces an abstract notion of game comparison, and a fundamental theorem gives an efficient play-comparison test. Game Reduction: Domination and Reversibility reduce games to unique canonical forms. Game Values: Games values are surreal numbers, switches, infinitesimals, dyadic rationals and more. Game Approximations: Temperature theory, reduced canonical form and atomic weights can be useful tools when the canonical for game value is too complex. Other Play Conventions: In addition to normal play, popular conventions are misere play, scoring play, auction play, etc. Reinforcement Learning and Combinatorial Games: We discuss a simple combinatorial game’s learning algorithm.

Description: Apart from their intrinsic role in the theory of stochastic processes, Markov chains and regenerative processes form an important set of tools for analysis and optimization problems arising in many decision models. Measure theoretic ideas of probability, expectation, convergence of random variables, limit theorems. Discrete time countable state Markov chains, hitting times, stopping times and strong Markov property. Recurrence and transience. Invariant measures for irreducible chains, ergodic theorem. Convergence in variation and coupling lemma. Absorption probabilities and criterion for transience. Discrete time renewal theory, elementary renewal theorem and renewal reward theorem. Regenerative processes and their time averages. Jump processes; jump chain and sojourn time construction of continuous time MCs, Poisson processes, birth-death processes. Forward and backward equations. Class structure, recurrence and transience, invariant distributions, convergence to equilibrium. Uniformization and time reversed chains. Optional: Martingales: conditional expectation, Martingale inequalities, Martingale convergence theorem, Brownian motion.

Description: Revised Syllabus: Aim of course: To familiarize students with implementation of optimization algorithms, combinatorial optimization problems, algorithms for statistics, machine learning and deep learning, algorithms for sampling, simulation, Bayesian inference, and other dynamical, stochastic models, using programming languages like Python, R and Matlab. Description: Outline: The proposed course will provide hands-on training on first-principles based state-of-the-art density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The setup of a basic planewave based-DFT calculator and the role of different simulation parameters on the obtained results would be discussed. The use of DFT calculator to calculate observable material properties such as bulk modulus, material density, speed of sound in materials, material stability, etc (without using any prior material knowledge) and their comparison with experimentally measured values (from textbook and literature) will be presented. The shortcomings of DFT calculations in predicting electronic bandgaps, handling strongly correlated solids (such as oxides) will be discussed. The course will conclude by presenting beyond-DFT machine learning based methods for accelerated material discovery. Students will work on individual projects where they will demonstrate the use of DFT calculation in their research and/or on an interesting scientific problem. Content: - Basics of programming in Python (different data types, loops, conditional execution, functions, modules, plotting), Python modules-numpy and matplotlib, introduction to atomic simulation environment (ase), ase visualization tools, introduction to unix-based HPC platform for calculations. - Introduction to crystal structures, lattice, basis, surfaces, interatomic interactions, force-fields, pair potentials, shortcomings of force-fields, introduction to DFT theory (basics only for completion). - Setting up DFT calculator via ASE-Python, choice and convergence of results with different DFT parameters, accuracy/speed trade-off, obtaining electronic energies and bandgaps. - Using DFT calculations to get Bulk modulus, material density, speed of sound, formation energies, and other observable material properties. - Under-prediction of electronic bandgaps, over/under bindings, strongly correlated solids, heavy atoms.

Description: The course is designed for students who are interested in understanding entrepreneurship, forming companies, affecting social impact through entrepreneurship, corporate innovation, or investing in startup ventures. Even if the student is not interested in starting a venture of their own, understanding the entrepreneurial process will enhance productivity even in large organizations. a) Students will learn an entrepreneurial framework by which to workshop an original idea, culminating in a 2-minute video elevator pitch competition. Student also will be given to understand the existing entrepreneurial ecosystem available in IITB-SINE. b) Students will practice evaluating other ideas by rating/judging peer 2-minute video pitches, and then teams will be formed around the best ideas. In addition, student teams will meet to prepare for their visit to the U.S. and to prepare for the June assignments (case studies and final pitch competition). c) Students will visit the St. Louis entrepreneurial ecosystem, meet with U.S. entrepreneurs and investors, engage in case study discussions, and compete in a final team-based pitch competition. d) Students who complete the course will have a thorough understanding of the various facets of entrepreneurship and the mindset of an entrepreneur; will refine their language and understanding of entrepreneurship; will understand how to evaluate new business opportunities; will learn how entrepreneurship incorporates and integrates other business disciplines in the development, management, and exit of a start-up venture; will understand how entrepreneurial principles might be used in other organizations; will understand the risks and rewards of pursuing opportunities in entrepreneurship and will be able to knowledgeably evaluate whether or not entrepreneurship may be a career interest. Class Time/Location: 8:30am-5pm:Two Days in the first of the program in Mumbai, Some asynchronous virtual coursework between sessions. 8:30-5pm: Two days in the last week of the program in St. Louis

Description: The objective of the course is to apply principles of muti-scale modelling to design of materials and materials processes. Materials design often involves understanding properties at disparate length and time-scales. Hence, modelling methods at multiple scales are required to bridge understanding across scales. The course contents will be delivered primarily through two or three case-studies. The problems could be related to either structural or functional aspects of materials. A case study will focus on either, 1. design of a material with target properties, or 2. design of a materials process Each case study is expected to span 4 - 6 weeks. It is expected that students will work in a collaborative mode. For a given problem/ case study, students are expected to integrate information flow between different techniques and across scales. Relevant concepts and tools for the required modelling methods will be introduced to the students. Each case study is split into weekly capsules. Multi-scaling and integration of techniques will be taught through weekly tutorials. Every tutorial will contribute to solving a specific aspect of the problem in the case study.

Description: The Berry phase, a fundamental geometric phase acquired by the wave function of a quantum system during adiabatic evolution, plays a crucial role in understanding a wide range of quantum phenomena. In quantum materials, it underpins the modern theory of polarization, anomalous Hall effects, and the topological classification of materials. By establishing a connection between the geometry of the wave function in momentum space and observable physical properties, the Berry phase provides deep insights into electronic polarization, anomalous Hall transport, and orbital magnetism. A key derivative of the Berry phase, the Berry curvature, acts as a fictitious magnetic field that governs the dynamics of quasi-particles, further enriching our understanding of quantum transport properties. Given its foundational significance, this course aims to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of Berry phase theory and its applications in topological systems, fer roelectrics, quantum Hall effects, and related transport phenomena.With increasing national and global emphasis on next-generation quantum materials, this course is particularly timely. By introducing students to these advanced concepts, it aims to motivate and prepare them for research in the evolving field of quantum materials.1) Introduction- Scope and objective, historical background2) Concept of Berry phase - Adiabatic theorem- Geometric phase- Berry Connection- Berry Curvature- Quantum metric3) Application of Berry phase to condensed matter systems(a) Topology - Topological invariant, Symmetry. - Quantum Hall effect, anomalous Hall effect. - Topological semi metals.(a) Topology - Topological invariant, Symmetry. - Quantum Hall effect, anomalous Hall effect. - Topological semi metals.(b) Electric polarization and orbital magnetization- Modern theory of polarization and orbital magnetization- Magneto electric effect and Axion coupling- Surface Anomalous Hall effect.4) Special topics in topology and geometry - Topology with disorder - Anderson insulators. - Manifestation of topology in Transport. - Interaction effects - Fractional quantum Hall, spin liquids- Topology in spin system - Magnon topology, Skyrmions.- Classification of topological insulators, superconductors.

Description: This course has three broad aims and several core objectives: 1. To make writing in general and policy related writing in particular, become a crucial tool for their professional development. 2. To introduce students to the theory and practice of narrative analysis and situated reading as a research methodology for interpreting texts. 3. To strengthen students’ ability to critique and problematise discourses through a critical reading of texts, identify gaps and raise relevant questions of discourses and themes represented within texts as works of art. This course will initiate students into the process of critique, evaluation and interpretation of pervasive discourses through the practice of textual analysis. The following are seven core objectives: Make students fluent in terms of writing and feel intellectually capacitated with Policy related themes. Make ‘writing’ become a very useful tool on their intellectual shelf. Familiarise students with the nuances of textual interpretation to aid discourse analysis. Introduce students to narratology, deep reading methods and humanities perspectives on discourse analysis. Enable students to think systematically, analytically and critically while interpreting texts through situated reading. Enable students to problematise texts and construct critiques of works, providing evidence for the critique from the text. Reflect on the ways in which textual interpretation in discourse analysis can enhance and deepen qualitative research practices. The topics covered in the course will include relevant contemporary themes from critical and cultural theory like the Anthropocene, construction of spaces, gender, conflict, globalization, diaspora and migration, and identity, among others. Relevant theorists and their works will be used alongside rhetorical works and artefacts like (non)fiction, memoirs, documentaries, films, to debate and construct critiques. Students will also be required to identify and use different rhetorical modes in their own writing and reflection pieces.
